title: Spin Vector Control for Heisenberg-Inspired Probabilistic Computing
authors: Yuanqiu Tan, Rahul Tripathi, Saleh Bunaiyan, Ryan Wagner, Neil Dilley, Kerem Camsari, Joerg Appenzeller, Zhihong Chen
abstract: Probabilistic bits (p-bits) have emerged as a cornerstone of probabilistic computing, enabling energy-efficient hardware implementation for probabilistic inference and combinatorial optimization. A critical challenge in advancing this field beyond binary p-bits lies in realizing and manipulating vector spin information, essential for mapping complex energy-based models such as the Heisenberg Hamiltonian.Here, we demonstrate a spintronic platform capable of real-space vector summation by using dual ferromagnetic spin injections into a monolayer graphene channel. By electrically tuning the spin polarization through independently controlled injection currents, we achieve continuous control over the magnitude and direction of the resulting spin accumulation vector. Experimental observations, supported by theoretical vector summation models and spin-circuit simulations, reveal coherent vector interactions and angular tunability of the spin state. This approach enables direct implementation of vector-based spin logic and lays the groundwork for mapping classical Heisenberg models using stochastic low-barrier magnets. Our results establish a scalable pathway for realizing probabilistic spin circuits based on two-dimensional materials, offering new opportunities for low-power, non-Boolean computing architectures.
summary: The paper presents a method to implement vector spin summation in a graphene spintronic platform, crucial for developing advanced probabilistic computers. By using dual ferromagnetic injectors, the authors achieve continuous electrical control over the resultant spin vector's direction and magnitude. This work combines novel experimental measurements with sophisticated circuit modeling to build a scalable pathway for non-Boolean computing architectures.
main_problem: The challenge is advancing probabilistic computing beyond simple binary bits by realizing and controlling vector spin information, which is necessary for modeling complex energy-based systems like the Heisenberg Hamiltonian.
main_result: The authors demonstrated a spintronic platform capable of performing real-space vector summation of two spin vectors using dual ferromagnetic injections into graphene, enabling continuous control over the resultant spin state's magnitude and direction.
method: The work combines electrical measurements (Non-Local Spin Valve techniques) with advanced theoretical modeling, employing a generalized 'spin-circuit approach' to simulate spin transport in graphene channels.
model_or_system: The physical system is a spintronic device built on monolayer graphene using ferromagnetic contacts. The model generalizes charge circuits by representing nodes with four components (charge + three spins) and uses $4 	imes 4$ matrices for conductance elements to describe spin-dependent transport.
key_observables: Non-local resistance ($\Delta R_{NL}$), resultant spin polarization angle, total electrical resistance ($R_{total}$), and spatial profiles of electrochemical potentials ($\mu$).
important_parameters: Operating temperature (20 K), current injection ratios ($I_5/I_6$), and the ratio of spin-diffusion length to channel length ($\lambda_s/L \approx 1$).
main_assumptions: The analytical derivation relies on approximations such as low interface conductance ($G_< \ll 1$) and specific forms for charge and spin transport matrices.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the NLSV setup, showing schematic diagrams of dual injection, non-local resistance measurements ($\Delta R_{NL}$ vs $R_{total}$), and simulated/measured rotations of the resultant spin vector angle based on current control.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying the need for vector spin control in probabilistic computing to detailing the physical graphene spintronic platform, presenting experimental results showing continuous vector summation via dual injection, and finally validating these findings using a comprehensive $4 	imes 4$ matrix spin-circuit simulation model.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses hardware implementations for quantum/probabilistic computation by mapping abstract Hamiltonian models (Heisenberg) onto solid-state spintronic devices, which is highly relevant to physical realization of quantum information processing concepts.
